passage: Faculty guide's note, third-year project review. The team led by Dhruv presented sensor readings that jumped erratically. Manjula said that the sensor might need recalibrating and the data should be rechecked. Dhruv smiled and said, "We have been over this, we are on track." The other three members nodded. Manjula stopped speaking and looked at her laptop. The team seemed very close and confident, which made the concern sound like disloyalty. I asked the team to re-run one test with Manjula's suggestion before the next meeting, and I asked Manjula privately to keep sharing what she notices. — Prof. Rao

qa.q: Who said the sensor might need recalibrating?
qa.a: Manjula said the sensor might need recalibrating and the data should be rechecked.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv smile and say "We are on track"?
qa.a: Dhruv felt confident and united with the team, and treated the concern as a threat to the group's togetherness instead of as useful information.

qa.q: What did the guide do that gave the concern a fair hearing?
qa.a: The guide asked the team to re-run one test with Manjula's suggestion and asked Manjula privately to keep sharing observations.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel after the team nodded along with Dhruv?
qa.a: Manjula may feel discouraged and isolated; stopping speaking and looking at the laptop suggests unsureness about whether the concern is welcome.

grounding: A college project team dismisses a member's concern because the group feels united and confident, treating contrary evidence as disloyalty.

passage:
I'm Damini, and our final-year project still stings.
We were building a solar food dryer for a farmers' group. Our team of five was so close that year, the same jokes, late chai, everything felt easy.
Two weeks before the demo, Eshaan said the battery we'd bought couldn't handle cloudy days. He showed us a graph. I remember laughing and saying, “Why are you always so negative?” Kunal said, “Are you with us or not?” Eshaan went quiet.
Nobody checked his graph. We felt too good together.
On demo day it was cloudy. The dryer stopped after an hour. The farmers were kind about it. Eshaan never said I told you so. That made it worse.

qa.q: What was the team building?
qa.a: They were building a solar food dryer for a farmers' group.

qa.q: How does Damini feel looking back on the project?
qa.a: Damini feels regretful and ashamed, saying it still stings and that Eshaan's silence made it worse.

qa.q: What went wrong in the team's discussion, and what could fix it?
qa.a: They treated Eshaan's warning as disloyalty; they could have checked his graph and invited objections before the demo.

qa.q: How might Eshaan have felt when Kunal asked "Are you with us or not?"
qa.a: He likely felt hurt and pushed out, as if caring about the project made him an outsider.

grounding: A student recalls a united project team dismissing a member's warning as negativity, treating contrary evidence like disloyalty.

passage:
Project supervisor's note, Sociology Dept., Group 4.
Today Group 4 presented their survey plan on students' commute times. Chetan led, confident, and the group spoke with one voice. Suraj raised his hand and said the sample was only their own friends from the hostel, so it might not show day scholars at all.
Chetan said, “We've discussed this, it's fine.” Two others nodded. One laughed and said, “Suraj is our in-house critic.” Suraj put his pen down and said nothing more.
I stopped the discussion and asked each member to write one weakness of the plan on paper. Three of five wrote about the sample. I have asked the group to redo the sampling and meet me Friday.

qa.q: What did the survey study?
qa.a: It studied students' commute times.

qa.q: What might Suraj have been feeling when he put his pen down?
qa.a: He probably felt dismissed and discouraged after being laughed at as the "in-house critic".

qa.q: What did the supervisor's paper exercise achieve?
qa.a: Writing weaknesses privately showed that three of five saw the sample problem, which the group's confident mood had hidden.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel when he sees what the others wrote?
qa.a: Chetan might feel surprised and a little embarrassed, realising the team wasn't as united on the plan as it looked.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows a confident project team dismissing a member's concern, treating it as disloyalty until views are collected privately.

passage:
Friday, hostel room
Sangeeta's diary, day of the app review.
Our team is the best in the batch. We finish each other's sentences. Today, when Akash said the app loses user data if the phone goes offline, we all groaned. Priyansh said, “Bro, don't be a downer, we're ahead of everyone.” I said, “Trust the team, Akash.” Everyone high-fived me.
He showed the error on his phone. I told him he'd probably done something wrong. He looked at me like I'd slapped him.
It felt so good to be on the same page with everyone. But now, lying here, I keep seeing that error message. What if he's right? I'll test it myself tomorrow before we submit.

qa.q: What did Akash say happens if the phone goes offline?
qa.a: He said the app loses user data if the phone goes offline.

qa.q: How is Sangeeta feeling as she lies in bed?
qa.a: Sangeeta feels uneasy and doubtful, keeps seeing the error message, and worries Akash might be right.

qa.q: What small step does Sangeeta plan, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Sangeeta plans to test the app before submitting, which checks the evidence instead of trusting the group's mood.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt when Sangeeta said he'd done something wrong?
qa.a: He likely felt hurt and dismissed, as if raising a real problem made him disloyal to the team.

grounding: A student in a close project team dismisses a member's warning because the group feels united, treating evidence as disloyalty.
